newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Activity seen stagnant all week.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Activity seen stagnant all week.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended in tight ranges on Monday and were expected to remain range bound on Tuesday as dealers had little new economic information on which to trade.

GovPX said Monday morning's trading volume was the lowest of the year. Few players were willing to place bets ahead of next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting and June nonfarm payrolls report.
The only data due on Tuesday were consumer confidence and readings on retail sales.
"There's nothing fundamental going on to shake up the markets this week," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.

Glassman said some people were looking to chain store sales on a week-to-week basis for signs of further slowing of the economy. Those figures provided a quick glimpse on economic strength, rather than monthly statistics, he said.

Car sales also were valuable in determining whether the Federal Reserve's policy makers would vote to further tighten monetary policy, Glassman said. The Fed tightened short-term interest rates by 25 basis points on March 25.

"Durable goods (scheduled for release on Wednesday) are interesting, but everybody already knows they're going to be strong," Glassman said. Economists polled by Reuters expected that, on average, May durable goods orders would rise by 0.6 percent following April's 1.3 percent increase.

News wires reported Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he hoped Japan and the U.S. would continue to cooperate on exchange rate stability with the goal of avoiding selling of U.S. Treasuries.
He said exchange rate instability could lead Japan to sell Treasuries and buy gold.
"(Tuesday) will be another day in a semi-quiet week. People will be looking at supply," said an economist at a primary dealership. He added he expected to see a continued downtrend in the economy.
While consumer confidence was at a 28-year high, that wasn't being translated to increased spending, he said.
"The big story is that before the FOMC meeting (July 1 and 2) nothing will happen," he said.
The Treasury was set to auction $15.5 billion of two-year notes on Tuesday and $11.5 billion of five-year notes on Wednesday.
The Treasury's 30-year bond was trading at 99-7/32, down 9/32, to yield 6.69 percent at the close on Monday.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum the three-month bill rate was up eight basis points at 5.02 percent. Six-month bills were up two basis points at 5.10 percent and year-bills were unchanged at 5.34 percent.
Five-year notes were down 2/32 at 100-28/32, yielding 6.29 percent. Ten-year notes were down 4/32 at 101-20/32, yielding 6.40 percent.
